title: I believe, we believe (CCC 166–167)
hook: faith is personal but never solitary

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four senses: literal, allegorical, moral, anagogical. Your line was one text, four depths. Today, the first words of the Creed.

A Sunday afternoon baptism. The baby is asleep, or furious. The priest turns to the parents and godparents and asks, one question at a time, whether they believe in God, the Father almighty, and in his Son, and in the Holy Spirit. Each time they answer out loud: I do. The next Sunday, at an ordinary Mass, the whole church stands and says the Creed together, every voice at once. Same faith. One time it sounds like a single voice; the next, like a crowd. Today: I believe, we believe.
screen: `A BAPTISM: I DO.` → `A SUNDAY MASS: EVERY VOICE AT ONCE.` → `I BELIEVE, WE BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: Day one hundred one took the Apostles' Creed line by line; today, just its first words. The Catechism notices the grammar. I believe is the faith of the Church professed by each believer personally, above all at baptism; that's how the Apostles' Creed speaks. We believe is the faith confessed by the bishops gathered in council, or by the whole assembly at worship; that's how the creed of the councils speaks. Both are true at once. Faith, the Catechism says, is a personal act: a person's free response to God who reveals himself. But it's never an isolated act. No one can believe alone, it says, just as no one can live alone. Nobody gave themselves faith, any more than they gave themselves life. It was received from others, and it's meant to be handed on. A moment in Mark's Gospel holds both sides. A father brings his son, who is suffering terribly, to Jesus. Jesus speaks of believing, and the father cries out, in the Douay-Rheims, "I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief." It's as personal as a sentence can be, and he says it in a crowd, on someone else's behalf, for his child. The Catechism recalls the baptism rite of the Roman Ritual, where the minister asks what is being sought from God's Church, and the answer is one word: faith. The Church, it says, believes first, and carries each believer. Even a private prayer, in the Catholic picture, is said inside a very large we.
screen: `I BELIEVE: EACH ONE, AT BAPTISM.` · `WE BELIEVE: THE CHURCH TOGETHER.` · `NO ONE BELIEVES ALONE.` · `I DO BELIEVE; HELP MY UNBELIEF.`

segments.voice: If you can, say the Creed with someone, at Mass, at home, or quietly along with a recording. If you're on your own, say or think the first two words, I believe, and let faces come to mind: the people whose faith reached you somehow, a grandparent, a teacher, a friend, a stranger in a pew. If you pray, thank God for them by name; if you don't, think of who carried what you know, in any part of life.
I believe. The first words of the Creed: personal, said by each one, and never said alone. Today's word.
Your line: no one believes alone. One voice at a baptism, a crowd on Sunday, the same faith. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: At baptism, the parents and godparents of a child, or the adult being baptized, profess the faith by answering the priest's questions; at Sunday Mass the congregation stands and says the Creed together.

chat.says: Isn't faith totally private? Why say the Creed out loud with a whole church?
options: The Catechism says faith is personal but never alone: it's received from others and said inside a we.
The Church says only the whole group believes; a single person can't really have faith of their own.
Because the Creed only counts when a priest leads it aloud; said alone at home, it means nothing.
chat.meaning: Faith is a personal act, a free response to God, but never isolated. The Catechism says no one believes alone, just as no one lives alone.

Catechism paraphrased (copyright): CCC 166 (personal act, not isolated; no one can believe alone as no one can live alone; faith received and handed on), CCC 167 ('I believe' and 'we believe'), CCC 168 (the Church believes first; the baptismal question and answer 'faith'). Confirm.

Hook: baptismal questions paraphrased loosely (renunciations omitted); in the current rite the parents' answer to 'what do you ask of God's Church' is usually 'baptism'; the fork therefore says 'the old baptismal rite the Catechism recalls'. Confirm.
Original: Latin 'Credo'; the note says it's why it's called a creed. That is an etymology claim not stated in CCC 166–167; Note now says only that it opens the Latin Apostles' Creed.
Practice adapted from the outline's 'pray the Creed with others' to 'say the Creed with others' so anyone can join.
